profile.name: box step
profile.tagline: A fundamental square-patterned dance step foundational to American Style ballroom.
profile.insight: Tracing a geometric square on the floor with full weight transfer, the box step anchors American Style waltz, rumba, and foxtrot.
profile.profile: The box step is a basic dance step named after the square or box pattern it traces on the floor. It is primarily utilized in American Style ballroom dances, including the rumba, waltz, and bronze-level foxtrot. While it can be performed individually, it is most commonly executed with a partner. Every step involves a full weight transfer, with rhythms varying across different dance styles.
profile.profile_long:
The box step is a foundational dance movement defined by the geometric square or box pattern it creates on the floor. It serves as a core component across several American Style ballroom dances, most notably as the most common dance step in the waltz, as well as in the rumba and bronze-level foxtrot. In international standard dance competition, a similar step is known as the closed change. 

In a typical execution, the leader begins with the left foot and proceeds through two distinct phases: the first half-box following a forward-side-together pattern, and the second half-box following a backwards-side-together pattern. Every step requires a full weight transfer. The underlying rhythm varies depending on the specific dance; for instance, it is counted as '1-2-3, 4-5-6' in the waltz, and 'slow quick quick, slow quick quick' in the rumba. In other variations, such as the quadrado figure of samba de Gafieira, the leader steps 'left-together-back, right-together-forward' starting with the left foot. 

Focusing on the waltz, the left box begins with the leader and follower starting with their feet closed. The leader steps forward on beat 1 with the left foot, steps to the side with the right on beat 2, and closes the left to the right on beat 3; then steps back with the right foot on beat 4, to the side with the left on beat 5, and closes the right to the left on beat 6. During the second and fifth steps, the foot travels along two sides of the box rather than along the diagonal. The follower mirrors this by starting with a step back on the right foot. The right box consists of the exact same steps mirrored, swapping the left and right feet for both partners. 

Beyond formal dance settings, the box step has appeared in popular culture, notably featured in an episode of the animated series Curious George titled 'School of Dance,' where the character George learns the step from the Renkins and teaches it to others.

sections.origins_and_history: The box step is a basic dance step originating as a foundational element in American Style ballroom dances. It is related to the closed change in international standard dance competition and shares a similar footprint pattern to the jazz box, albeit with cross-steps.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The step is performed individually or with a partner. In a typical example, the leader starts with the left foot. The first half-box is forward-side-together, and the second half-box is backwards-side-together, with full weight transfer on every step. In the waltz left box, the leader steps forward-left, side-right, close-left-to-right, then back-right, side-left, close-right-to-left. The follower mirrors this starting with the right foot. In samba de Gafieira's quadrado, the pattern is left-together-back, right-together-forward.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Used in American Style ballroom dancing, partner dancing, dance competitions, and featured in popular culture such as an episode of Curious George titled 'School of Dance'.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include the waltz left box and right box, the rumba box step variation, bronze-level foxtrot applications, and the quadrado figure in samba de Gafieira.
sections.lineage: Related to the closed change in international standard dance and the jazz box step.

basic_steps: Step forward with the left foot (beat 1)
Step to the side with the right foot (beat 2)
Close the left foot to the right foot (beat 3)
Step back with the right foot (beat 4)
Step to the side with the left foot (beat 5)
Close the right foot to the left foot (beat 6)
